newsitem.title: EGYPT: Mubarak, Arafat mull not going to U.S. summit.
newsitem.headline: Mubarak, Arafat mull not going to U.S. summit.

text.p: Egyptian and Palestinian Presidents Hosni Mubarak and Yasser Arafat mulled a revolt against U.S. diplomacy on Monday, casting doubt on plans for a Middle East summit in Washington on Tuesday.

Arafat flew to see Mubarak in the northwest Egyptian town of Burg al-Arab and Palestinian officials said Arafat had asked U.S. President Bill Clinton to postpone his plans for the summit with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyhau.
Mubarak has been even more reluctant to go, on suspicion that Clinton and Netanyahu will not give the Arabs credible guarantees that Israel will carry out old agreements.
Diplomatic sources said that unless Netanyahu backed down on his refusal to reach any agreement before the summit, it was hard to see how Arafat and Mubarak could attend.

"Mubarak wants to see a clearly defined programme of action (by Israel). And he doesn't want to get involved in an unsuccessful summit," said an Arab diplomat close to the Arafat-Mubarak talks in Burg al-Arab.
"So far the Israelis are still being intransigent. Contacts are continuing but the position is not clear," he added.
The Palestinian ambassador to the Arab League, Mohamed Sobeih, said there was a strong possibility Arafat would fly to Brussels later on Monday but not necessarily en route for Washington.
The Arab stand amounts to a revolt against Washington unprecedented since the United States brought Israel and its Arab neighbours together at the Madrid conference in 1991.

It also shows the depth of Arab disillusionment with the U.S. administration, which has declined to take a stand in public against the policies of Netanyahu's rightwing government, which came to power after elections in May.
Palestinian officials said an all-night meeting between Palestinians, Israelis, U.S. and U.N. officials failed to solve problems over what the summit would discuss.

Arafat and Mubarak want Israel to close a tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Arab East Jerusalem, which Israel captured in the 1967 Middle East war. Netanyahu says the controversial tunnel will stay open forever and this is not on the agenda.
"The idea was to agree on most everything here before going to Washington, but no conclusions were reached," said Marwan Kanafani, an Arafat aide.

"The Israelis refused to agree on any political issues. They wanted to discuss security issues. They are not serious, and Arafat has no desire to meet Netanyahu just for the sake of meeting him," added a PLO official who declined to be named.
Clinton called for the summit to help end five days of clashes in which 55 Palestinians and 14 Israelis have died.
The clashes broke out after Israel opened the tunnel near the Aqsa mosque in Jerusalem, Islam's third holiest site.

"The loss of life and the tragedy of the violence in the Middle East this week have been a terrible development for the Israeli and the Palestinian people, a blow to all those who have worked for a lasting peace, an encouragement to those who oppose a lasting peace," Clinton said.
But in an interview published on Monday, Mubarak said that unless Netanyahu carries out agreements signed by Israel and the Palestinian Authority, the violence could break out again.
"The situation can explode again, as long the agreements and treaties are not implemented," he told the party newspaper Mayo.

"The latest events in the Palestinian territories are the natural result of procrastination in carrying out the articles of the agreements and the severe pressure on the economy of the Palestinian people," he added.
"I have warned before and I warn again of a new uprising by the Palestinians if they are in despair or lose hope that they will obtain their rights, as enshrined in charters.
Clinton, U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, King Hussein of Jordan and Israeli President Ezer Weizman called Mubarak on Sunday to try to persuade him to Washington.
King Hussein left for Washington on Monday regradless of the last-minute demands of Arafat and Mubarak.
